content: The oxeye daisy, scientifically known as Leucanthemum vulgare (synonym Chrysanthemum leucanthemum), is a flowering plant native to Europe and temperate regions of Asia. It is commonly referred to as the marguerite and is one of several plants known by the common name daisy. Additionally, it is sometimes called the moon daisy or dog daisy. This plant is a perennial herb that grows prostrate and produces small flower heads, typically no larger than 5 cm in diameter. Each flower head consists of approximately 20 white ray florets surrounding numerous yellow disc florets, which are borne at the end of the stem. The stem is predominantly unbranched and grows laterally from a creeping rootstock. The leaves are dark green on both sides, with basal and middle leaves being petiolate, obovate to spoon-shaped, and serrate to dentate. The upper leaves are shorter, sessile, and grow along the stem. The oxeye daisy produces a large number of flat seeds that lack a pappus. It also propagates vegetatively through rooting underground stems. This plant is a characteristic meadow flower, thriving in diverse plant communities such as dry fields, meadows, areas under shrubs, open-canopy forests, and waste places. It is highly adaptable to a wide range of environmental conditions but shows a preference for heavy and damp soils. The oxeye daisy has been introduced to parts of North America, Australia, and New Zealand, where it has become a common weed. In some areas, it displaces native plant species and is challenging to control or eradicate due to its ability to regenerate from rhizome fragments. Despite this, in North Carolina, it is intentionally planted along roadsides by the highway department. The unopened flower buds of the oxeye daisy can be pickled and used as a substitute for capers. Additionally, this flower is associated with the traditional game He loves me, he loves me not, known in French as effeuiller la marguerite.
